title: Conseguir --- Getting Is Following Until You Have It

lessons.title: conseguir — "to get", by following a thing until you have it
lessons.gloss: to get, to obtain — getting as following a thing until you have it

segments.text: Traigo carries a thing that is already yours. Coger grabs what is in front of you. This verb is for the getting that took some work.
g-hard — the gu in conseguir is one hard g; the u is silent.
s-clear — a clean hissing s: con-se-GEER.
conseguir ("to get, to obtain, to manage to") from Latin cōnsequī: com- ("along with") + sequī, "to follow". You got a thing by following it until it was yours.

Sequī is one of Latin's great English suppliers: sequence, sequel, consequence, subsequent, consecutive; second, from secundus, "the one following"; execute and prosecute; obsequious, following someone about; and through French, pursue, ensue and suit.
Spanish also keeps the formal partner obtener from obtinēre, "to hold onto" — English obtain. It behaves exactly like tener, so its yo-form is obtengo. Conseguir is the everyday one.

blocks.title: Grammar Lens: the third crack, and a silent u that leaves

segments.text: You have met dormir breaking o becomes ue and pido quietly breaking e becomes i. Here is that third pattern in full: stress on the stem turns e into i, and conseguimos stays plain because the stress moved to the ending.

Now the spelling. Spanish writes gu only to keep a g hard in front of e and i. Once the e becomes i, there is nothing in front to guard against, so the u has no job and goes: consigo, not consiguo. Two changes, one form, and only one of them is a sound.

segments.instruction: "Traigo el café" then "Consigo el café" — carried, then obtained
segments.source: [YOU SAY: "Traigo el café" then "Consigo el café" — carried, then obtained]

segments.text: What did sequī mean, and name two English words from it. (To follow; sequence, second, consequence, pursue.) Why is it consigo and not consiguo? (The u only guards a hard g before e and i.) Name the three stem cracks you now have, with a verb for each. (Cerrar e becomes ie, dormir o becomes ue, conseguir e becomes i.) And which Latin verb is behind traer? (Trahere.)
